extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and logic; logicians; anyone studying analysis of propositions
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze what propositions assert (their immediate object) and how predication works: classify proposition-types, distinguish meanings derived from connotation vs denotation, and avoid common theoretical errors (e.g., treating reasoning as mere manipulation of ideas or fixed class-lists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate object of belief (proposition's matter-of-fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proposition is asserted, its immediate object is the facts or phenomena themselves (the things, occurrences, or states of consciousness), not merely the mental ideas or names corresponding to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze propositions as referring to natural phenomena (e.g., 'fire causes heat' refers to the natural phenomena, not merely ideas of fire and heat). Treat believing and asserting as acts about the facts; avoid the error of reducing judgment to operations on ideas alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-fold classification of matters-of-fact
rubrics_metrics.description: All substantive propositions (not merely verbal ones) assert one of five kinds of matter-of-fact: Existence, Co-existence, Sequence, Causation, or Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this exhaustive classification to identify what a proposition is claiming: existence of something; co-existence (simultaneity); sequence (order in time); causation (one phenomenon producing another); or resemblance (likeness of sensations/objects). Examples and distinctions follow in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation over denotation (meaning resides in attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For general (connotative) names the real meaning lies in the connotation—i.e., the attributes a name implies—rather than merely the set of objects it denotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing propositions like 'All men are mortal', focus on the attributes connoted by 'man' and 'mortal' and their regular conjunction in phenomena, not on a pre-existing list of individuals. Discoveries (e.g., diamond combustibility) show class-membership follows from attributes uncovered by observation, not from name-lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of Hobbes' name-identity theory of predication
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes's claim that a proposition simply states that the predicate is 'a name of the same thing' as the subject is only adequate when both subject and predicate are proper names; it fails for most predications involving connotative terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Hobbes's analysis only to identity-predications between proper names (e.g., 'Tully is Cicero'). For predicates that connote attributes, Hobbes's account is 'sadly inadequate'—meaning analysis must look to connotation and the facts that ground it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names vs connotative names
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names are mere marks for individuals and carry (strictly) no meaning; connotative (general/abstract) names connote attributes and thus ground substantive predications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subject or predicate is a proper name, predication reduces to identity-marking; when connotative, analyze the connoted attributes and the phenomena that justify predication. Do not treat all names as if they behaved like proper names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal vs real questions (source of falsity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some false propositions arise from ignorance or misuse of language (verbal falsity), while others are false from misapprehension of facts (real falsity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether disagreement comes from meanings of words or from disagreement about the facts denoted/connoted. This distinction prevents conflating linguistic mistakes with substantive errors about the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification is grounded in attributes and observation, not antecedent rolls
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes are not fixed lists of individuals predetermined by framers of language; they are formed by reference to attributes, and class-membership may change as new observations reveal attributes in previously unclassified objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the anti-pattern of treating classification as reading a pre-existing record of which individuals belong to which class. Use empirical investigation of attributes to justify including objects in classes (example: discovering that diamond is combustible led to its inclusion under relevant class-properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Order in Place vs Co-inherence of Attributes (and Order in Time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions of co-existence divide into (a) Order in Place—arrangements taking account of place (spatial ordering), and (b) Co-inherence of Attributes—the concurrence of attributes/functions in the same part or locality; both contrast with Order in Time (sequence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Bain's distinction: spatially ordered facts (places/positions) differ from co-inherence where multiple properties coexist in the same entity (e.g., hardness, color, lustre in every atom of gold). Co-inherence may be potential and belongs to simultaneity/time rather than place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borderline class-membership often only asserts resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: When objects lie near the boundary of a class (anomalous genera/species), predication may amount merely to asserting resemblance to the class rather than unequivocal possession of its defining attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In borderline cases qualify predication with phrases like 'is considered' or 'may be ranked'; recognize that sometimes predicating a class-name means the object either possesses the class-properties or at least resembles the class more than alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertions about noumena/substances are grounded in phenomena (predicated causation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When propositions appear to assert existence or properties of noumena/substances (things-in-themselves), their meaningful content is grounded in the observable phenomena by which those substances manifest themselves; asserting a noumenon's existence effectively asserts causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims about substances as claims about the series of observable facts they produce or the states of consciousness they accompany. In effect, asserting a noumenon invokes a causal claim linking it to observable phenomena.
